# V (Visa Inc.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand: Visa runs a global payments network, taking a small fee on transaction volume that flows over its rails, while issuing banks (not Visa) bear the consumer credit risk. There is no black-box financial engineering and no meaningful technology risk in the traditional sense — this is squarely in the 'easy pile.'

## Moat & Durability — Score 9/10
Visa's moat is a genuine two-sided network effect: more cardholders make the network more valuable to merchants, and more merchant acceptance makes cards more valuable to cardholders, a flywheel that is extremely expensive for a new entrant to replicate. Scale (thousands of issuing banks, tens of millions of merchants globally), brand trust, and a near-duopoly structure with Mastercard have kept this moat intact for decades against serial waves of would-be disruptors (PayPal, crypto, fintech wallets), most of which ended up riding Visa's rails rather than replacing them. The two live threats are regulatory (interchange caps, mandated routing competition) and technological (real-time account-to-account payment rails, stablecoins, domestic schemes like Pix), neither of which has dented Visa's volume growth to date but both of which are credible decade-scale risks, hence 9 rather than 10.

## Management & Capital Allocation
A 61.2% ROE combined with a 66.1% operating margin and 97.7% gross margin implies management runs an extraordinarily capital-light, high-return business and reinvests selectively rather than empire-building. Debt/equity of roughly 68% is moderate, not aggressive — the high ROE looks driven by margin structure and buyback-shrunk equity rather than leverage. What this packet cannot show: actual buyback pace, dividend payout ratio, executive comp structure, or M&A discipline on smaller fintech/infrastructure acquisitions Visa periodically makes. Treat 'trustworthy management' as a reasonable inference from the capital-efficiency numbers, not a verified fact.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 14.4% on an already-massive, dominant network is a notable data point — this is not a business squeezing out growth from a shrinking base, it reflects genuine secular tailwinds (e-commerce penetration, cross-border travel recovery, tap-to-pay/contactless adoption) plus pricing power. Visa carries no consumer credit risk, removing the single largest source of earnings volatility that hits card-issuing banks in a downturn. Momentum is unremarkable rather than confirmatory: 1-month +0.2%, 3-month +13.5%, 6-month +13.1%, 12-month +7.5%, RSI 54.7 (neutral), momentum score 54.8/100. The packet's thesis field is null, so there's no fresh qualitative signal reinforcing the growth trend — predictability here rests on the historical numbers and business model logic, not on independently confirmed forward guidance.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Regulatory compression**: interchange-fee caps spreading to more jurisdictions, forced network-routing competition (Durbin-style rules elsewhere), or a DOJ/EU merchant-litigation loss directly cuts Visa's take rate on volume it doesn't control pricing for unilaterally.
2. **Rail disintermediation**: real-time account-to-account payments, stablecoins, and domestic instant-payment schemes (FedNow-style, Pix-style) increasingly bypass card networks for both retail and cross-border transactions, eroding volume growth in Visa's highest-margin corridors over a multi-year horizon.
3. **Macro/multiple double-hit**: a global recession or sharp cross-border travel pullback hits the highest-margin cross-border fee revenue hardest at the same moment the market's premium multiple (31x trailing P/E, ~22x EV/EBITDA, 3.0% FCF yield) has zero room to absorb a growth miss — the earnings hit and the multiple compression would arrive together.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($679.9B), trailing P/E (31.04x), forward P/E (24.32x), EV/EBITDA (21.9x), and FCF yield (3.0%) but not share price or share count directly. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~2.02B diluted share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $336.6/share, trailing EPS near $10.85, forward EPS near $13.84, and FCF/share near $10.10 — call normalized owner earnings roughly $10.00/share after a modest haircut for stock-based comp.

Applying an owner-earnings multiple range appropriate for a wide-moat, capital-light network compounder growing low-to-mid teens:
- **Low case** (26x owner earnings, reflecting real regulatory/rail-disruption risk over the next decade): ~$260/share.
- **High case** (33x owner earnings, if the duopoly moat and double-digit growth persist largely unchallenged): ~$330/share.

Midpoint ~$295/share vs. an implied current price of ~$336.6/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-12%** — the price is running ahead of a conservative owner-earnings estimate, not behind it. This is a 'wonderful business, full price' situation rather than a bargain: Visa's economics are as good as they come, but the current price already assumes a great deal of that quality persists uninterrupted for years.

## The Cloning Caveat
This is an unusually strong convergence of respected investors. Bill Ackman (Pershing Square) opened a new position at 5.76% of portfolio — a real, high-conviction bet from a concentrated activist who rarely holds more than a handful of names. Seth Klarman (Baupost) opened a new 4.14% position — notable because Baupost is known for deep-value, often distressed situations, so a mega-cap quality compounder entering at this size is a real signal about price/quality tradeoff, not habit. ValueAct added 34.8% to reach 3.17%, and Viking Global added 58.83% to reach 1.98% — both building, not just initiating. Chris Hohn (TCI), Chase Coleman (Tiger Global), Dodge & Cox, Glenn Greenberg (Brave Warrior), and a long tail of smaller managers round out the list. Read collectively: a genuinely broad, high-quality investor base is accumulating Visa right now, which corroborates the business-quality thesis strongly — but it does not resolve the valuation question. Even Ackman and Klarman paying up for quality is a bet that these economics persist, not proof that today's price offers a margin of safety.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 6/10.** Visa is about as close to an ideal business as this framework identifies — a durable network moat, minimal capital needs, no credit risk, and elite margins/returns on capital, corroborated by an unusually broad and credible set of superinvestor buyers. But Munger and Buffett both insist on a price that leaves room for error, and by a conservative owner-earnings estimate this packet implies Visa is trading roughly 12% above fair value, not below it. This belongs on the short list to buy aggressively on any real pullback (a market drawdown, a regulatory scare, a growth-deceleration quarter) rather than a name to chase at the current price.

value-investor cluster rather than a momentum crowd. The stock is up 13.5% over 3 months and
13.1% over 6 months but essentially flat over the last month (+0.23%), and 12-month return
(7.5%) trails both, meaning the bulk of the move happened earlier and price has spent the
recent stretch consolidating 10.7% above its 200DMA rather than extending — a healthy pause,
not distribution, given RSI14 sits at a neutral 54.7 with no overbought unwind pending. There
is no short-squeeze mechanic here (1.2% of float short, 2.6 days to cover) — that's simply
structural for a mega-cap, low-beta (0.76) compounder, not a bearish tell, and the composite is
arguably over-penalizing that absence. Options positioning is unremarkable (put/call OI 0.95,
near parity), so there's no crowd enthusiasm via derivatives defending the level. What actually
differentiates this tape is the buy-side: Ackman initiated a 5.76%-of-portfolio position and
Klarman a 4.14% stake, while ValueAct (+34.8%), Viking Global (+58.8%), TCI (+9.9%), and
roughly a dozen other quality/value shops added across both Q1 and Q2 2026 filings — a
multi-quarter, multi-manager consensus around a 97.7%-gross-margin, 61% ROE toll-booth
business, not a single momentum-chasing print. That buying is a lagging, fundamentals-driven
signal that provides a sticky ownership base and downside floor, but it is not itself a
forward price catalyst, so the flat 1-month tape should be read as digestion of the Q2
re-rating while the market waits for the next print to confirm the thesis.
